summary: Registers the MIME sub-type image/tiff-fx, whose encodings are defined by the File Format for Internet Fax and its extensions.

plainLanguage.summary: It is a name tag, image/tiff-fx, that tells email programs what kind of fax picture file is inside a message.

questions: what is the tiff-fx file extension
when to use image/tiff instead of image/tiff-fx
subtitle: Registers image/tiff-fx, the MIME type for Internet fax image files.

tldr.problem: Mail and other systems need a registered media type name to label TIFF-FX fax image files, so receivers know what kind of data they have.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC registers the MIME sub-type image/tiff-fx, with no parameters, binary encoding, magic numbers for the file header and the file extension .TFX. The encodings themselves are defined in RFC 3949.
tldr.outcome: image/tiff-fx covers TIFF-FX Profiles J, C, L and M, while image/tiff stays the preferred type for black-and-white Profiles S and F. It obsoletes RFC 3250.

today: RFC 3950 is a Draft Standard that obsoletes RFC 3250. The unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it, and the format it registers is defined in RFC 3949.

sections.title: What the Registration Is For
sections.content:
RFC 3950 describes the registration of the MIME sub-type image/tiff-fx. The encodings are defined by RFC 3949, File Format for Internet Fax, and its extensions. The document is a product of the IETF Internet Fax Working Group.

It gives only a brief scope and feature description as background. Tag Image File Format Fax eXtended (TIFF-FX) is defined in detail by RFC 3949, and readers are directed there for complete technical details.
sections.plainLanguage: When a fax picture travels in an email, it needs a label on the outside. This document makes that label official.

sections.title: TIFF-FX in Brief
sections.content:
TIFF-FX is a TIFF-based file format for messaging-based fax over the Internet. It specifies the TIFF fields and values needed for compatibility with ITU-T Recommendations for Group 3 black-and-white, grayscale and color facsimile. It recommends a file structure compatible with low-memory and page-level streaming implementations.

The RFC lists three features: it can describe bilevel, grayscale, palette-color, full-color and mixed content image data; it includes several compression schemes so developers can choose a space or time tradeoff; and it is designed to be extensible and to evolve gracefully.
sections.plainLanguage: TIFF-FX is the picture file format fax pages use. It can handle plain black-and-white pages as well as colorful ones.

sections.title: Which Type for Which Profile
sections.content:
The image/tiff-fx type refers to TIFF-FX Profiles J, C, L and M encoded image data, any future TIFF-FX extensions, or a subset. For black-and-white data encoded with Profiles S or F, or a subset, the image/tiff-fx type MAY be used, but the image/tiff content type SHOULD be used instead.

The Annex notes that this SHOULD was added relative to RFC 3250 to stress that image/tiff is the preferred type for Profiles S and F.
sections.plainLanguage: Simple black-and-white faxes should wear the ordinary picture label. The fancier fax files get the special tiff-fx label.

sections.title: The IANA Registration
sections.content:
The registration template gives the type as image and the sub-type as tiff-fx, with no required and no optional parameters. The type consists of binary data, so base64 should be used on transports that cannot carry binary directly. The published specification is RFC 3949.

Files carry magic numbers: 49 49 2A 00 in hex for little-endian (II) and 4D 4D 00 2A for big-endian (MM). The file extension is .TFX, the Macintosh file type code is TFX, and the intended usage is COMMON. The change controller is Lloyd McIntyre. The registration lists imaging, fax, messaging and multi-media as applications that use the type.

For interoperability, the RFC warns that support for every application or profile of TIFF-FX may not be ubiquitous, so an implementation may decode and try to display an image only to find it cannot render it.
sections.plainLanguage: The registration card lists the label's name, how to spot the file by its first bytes, and what to call the file on disk.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The fields defined in TIFF-FX are descriptive and help a recipient view and render an image. They are not used to induce any particular behavior by the recipient application, so they do not by themselves create additional security risks.

Because TIFF-FX is extensible, the RFC acknowledges it is theoretically possible that fields could be defined later that induce actions by the recipient. That is not supported by the referenced specification, and defining such fields would be inconsistent with the goals and spirit of TIFF-FX. The MIME type and file extension MUST NOT be used to blindly select a processing program; the implementation decides which application, if any, to use and renders the image to the user.
sections.plainLanguage: The file only describes a picture. Do not let the file's name or label decide which program runs, because the receiving program should choose for itself.
